questions.q: What are the three dimensions that define a 3D shape?
questions.a: The three dimensions are length, width, and depth (or height). A wrong answer suggests the student is still thinking in terms of 2D shapes, which only have length and width.

questions.q: If you hold a ball, does it have any edges or vertices? Explain why.
questions.a: No, a sphere has no edges or vertices because it has a perfectly smooth, curved surface with no flat faces meeting. A student saying it has "one edge" is confusing the curvature of the object with a linear edge.

questions.q: A cuboid has 6 faces. If you paint all the faces of a cuboid, how many edges would you need to be careful not to get paint on if you were only handling it by the lines where the faces meet?
questions.a: You would need to watch out for 12 edges. Counting faces and edges accurately requires visualizing the 3D structure; an incorrect answer suggests the student is miscounting or missing hidden edges.

questions.q: Compare a cylinder and a cone. How are their circular faces different in terms of how they meet other parts of the shape?
questions.a: A cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface, whereas a cone has only one circular face that tapers into a single point (vertex). Confusing these suggests the student isn't visualizing the tapering effect of a cone.

questions.q: Can a pyramid have a circular base? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, by definition, a pyramid has a polygon base (a shape with straight edges) and triangular faces that meet at a point. If the base were circular, it would be a cone, not a pyramid.

questions.q: Describe a new 3D object found in your kitchen that is not a cube or sphere, and identify its faces, edges, and vertices.
questions.a: A good answer would describe a cereal box (cuboid) with 6 rectangular faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices. An incomplete answer shows the student has not yet generalized the definition to objects beyond the textbook examples.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Three-______ (3D) shapes are solid objects that occupy space and possess three dimensions: length, width, and depth (or height).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are holding your ______ box or an ice cream cone; have you ever noticed why these objects feel solid while a drawing on your notebook looks flat?
Fill in the blank: Three-dimensional (______D) shapes are solid objects that occupy space and possess three dimensions: length, width, and depth (or height).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to correctly identify 3D shapes in real-world objects and name their components (faces, edges, and vertices) for cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, and spheres.
